overview: Frankish kingdoms grew within the former Roman world and became major powers in western Europe. Their history includes the Merovingian dynasty, the Carolingian takeover in 751 and Charlemagne’s rise. Wooden farms, jeweled fasteners, books and seal rings reveal lives beyond the battlefield. These two map entries cover successive stretches of a longer history; neither 600 nor 800 marks the disappearance of Frankish communities.

periods.title: Roman connections and expanding kingdoms
periods.summary: Frankish leaders served in Roman armies and established kingdoms. Clovis expanded his rule before his death in 511.

periods.title: Merovingian kingdoms
periods.summary: Clovis’s sons divided his kingdom. Merovingian rulers governed a world whose crafts and everyday life retained Roman influences.

periods.title: The Carolingian royal dynasty
periods.summary: Pepin replaced the last Merovingian king in 751. Charlemagne became king in 768 and emperor in 800.

sections.title: Rulers, families and a changing kingdom

items.text: Frankish soldiers served in Roman armies, and some leaders rose within the imperial military. Their kingdoms developed through both cooperation and conflict with Rome. They were not modern France or Germany with familiar national borders.

Clovis defeated Syagrius at Soissons in 486. His victory over the Visigoths near Poitiers in 507 extended Frankish power into Aquitaine. Conquest helped create a powerful kingdom, but did not instantly replace the people living there.

Royal marriages were political relationships too: Clovis married Clotilde, a relative of the Burgundian king. When Clovis died in 511, four sons shared his kingdom. One royal family could therefore produce several royal courts.

Clovis became Christian, but the exact date of his baptism is disputed. Surviving accounts were written for different purposes, often much later. A neat date in a school timeline can hide a real historical puzzle.

By the late seventh century, powerful officials called mayors of the palace increasingly overshadowed the Merovingian kings. Pepin the Short removed the last Merovingian ruler in 751 and founded the Carolingian royal dynasty.

sections.title: Homes, food and neighbors with hooves

items.text: At Les Gravilliers near Pontarlier, a settlement occupied during the sixth and seventh centuries had about ten large wooden buildings, each roughly 200-300 square metres. Archaeologists identify divided living quarters in one part and room for livestock in another. Some neighbors apparently came with hooves.

Storage buildings surrounded those houses. Thousands of cattle and horse bones lay in a large slaughtering and butchery area. The findings show how central livestock were to this particular settlement’s work and food supply; they do not give us a menu for every Frankish household.

The Pontarlier settlement also had a wooden church and graves close to the houses. Jewelry and swords in some burials suggest wealthy residents. Archaeologists propose that several graves near the church belonged to a founding family, but that relationship is an interpretation, not a recovered family tree.

Most people lived in the countryside. Small farms existed beside estates controlled by rulers, churches and aristocrats. Work involved crops, animals and crafts; bishops and older towns also remained important to administration and economic life.

At Pontarlier, the excavators found no sign of violent destruction when the settlement was abandoned. They suggest possibilities including a move toward the nearby town or changes in the estate economy. An abandoned village is not automatically the scene of a battle.

The published Pontarlier accounts used here describe buildings, burials and animal remains but do not establish the residents’ toilet arrangements. That gap does not tell us that toilets were absent. A convincing bathroom story needs evidence of its own.

sections.title: Getting dressed and making beautiful things

items.text: The Met’s account of Frankish dress describes women wearing belted tunics with a wrap or cloak, plus jewelry and pendants suspended from belts. Small paired brooches fashionable in earlier centuries gave way to large single disk brooches during the 600s. Fasteners could do the job of both a pin and a jewel.

A surviving Frankish brooch from the middle of the 600s, now at the Met, combines gold, garnets, colored glass and mother-of-pearl in a disk only 4.4 centimetres across. Such fine work reveals skilled craftspeople and wealthy customers. The museum’s acquisition date does not identify an ancient excavation site.

Brussels’s Art & History Museum reconstructs graves from Harmignies in present-day Belgium. Wood and clothing have generally decayed, while bone, glass and metal objects survive more often. What archaeologists recover is therefore only part of what people originally wore or owned.

The same museum uses archaeological evidence to reconstruct a textile workshop and a house under construction. Its collections also show work in glass, pottery, bone and metal. Producing everyday clothes and containers required skills alongside the spectacular goldsmithing that catches our eye.

sections.title: Learning, books and caring for the sick

items.text: Merovingian monasteries copied books by hand, with workshops at places including Corbie, Tours and Luxeuil. They developed different handwriting styles rather than using one uniform script. The BnF identifies surviving manuscripts and fragments as direct evidence of this work.

Classical authors such as Virgil and Cicero remained part of elite education. The royal court attracted people who could read and write, and some kings wrote too. This evidence of learned circles does not mean that every child attended school.

Medical learning did not simply vanish after Roman rule. Historian James Palmer’s study of early manuscripts traces medical knowledge in Merovingian Gaul and its place within broader education. Religious study and learning about the body could overlap.

Palmer also examines how people understood miraculous cures, nature and the failure of medicine during epidemics. These sources reveal efforts to explain illness, not proof that every remedy worked. Beliefs about healing and the results of treatment are different kinds of evidence.

CHILDIRICI REGIS means “of King Childeric.” This Latin inscription appeared around the portrait on Childeric’s fifth-century seal ring, found in his grave at Tournai in 1653. The wording helped identify the burial. It is an attested royal inscription, not a newly invented Frankish greeting.

The original ring was stolen in 1831 and did not survive; earlier records and later reproductions preserve its appearance. A 1924 museum guide explicitly labels the displayed ring an electrotype facsimile. The ancient text survives through documentation, even when the ancient object does not.

Childeric’s grave also contained weapons and richly decorated fittings, including small gold ornaments shaped like insects. The combination of Roman and Germanic symbols helps explain a ruler whose authority connected both worlds. A royal tomb is exceptional evidence, not an ordinary family’s belongings.

Another signet ring, from seventh-century northern France and now at the Met, is made of electrum and carries a monogram. Rings could stamp personal seals on documents. Its museum entry does not decode this particular monogram, so we should not invent the owner’s name.

Charlemagne became king of the Franks in 768. His court drew scholars from several regions and supported books, churches and clearer handwriting. The later Carolingian cultural revival built on existing traditions of learning and skilled craftsmanship.

Pope Leo III crowned Charlemagne emperor on Christmas Day in 800. This marks the next imperial phase of Frankish political history, represented by a separate map entry. It was a change in royal status, not the extinction of the Franks.

The National Archaeology Museum emphasizes that the dynasty change is much less obvious in daily life than in royal history. Farms, skills and communities did not all restart when a new family took the throne. The year 600 likewise divides these map records, not two unrelated peoples.

ending.text: Merovingian royal rule ended in 751 when Pepin took the throne. Under the Carolingians, Charlemagne became emperor in 800. Frankish society continued through these political changes; the map’s 600 and 800 boundaries are divisions between records, not dates when a people disappeared.
